c: Our second panel moves from principles to practice.
What would embedded third-party evaluators and pre-release testing through global standard bodies
actually require of industry, of institutions and of science? What are the requirements?
So leading the conversation is our friend Claire Melamed,
Vice President for AI and Digital Cooperation at
the United Nations Foundation. Claire, thank you.
She is joined on stage by Professor Yoshua
Bengio, co-president and scientific director of LawZero
and co-chair of the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI.
His other co-chair unfortunately couldn’t make it tonight, and she’s sending her regrets.
Then it’s followed by our friend Jaan Tallinn, who’s the co-founder of Skype,
co-founder of Kazaa, but also co-founder of the Future of Life Institute. Jaan.
Xiao Qian, Vice Dean at Tsinghua University for AI International Governance and Deputy Director
for the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua.
And lastly, our friend Sara Rendtorff-Smith, Head of AI and Emerging Digital Technologies
Division at the OECD. Claire, over to you.
A very warm welcome to you all. It’s an absolute
honor to be here with this stellar panel. Before
we start, though, I just want to give everyone a
little break and just urge you all, if you’re
not already looking that way, just turn around
and look out the window. It’s so stunning.
I mean, look at that. Yeah. Okay. Now you’ve had your aesthetic pleasure,
let us go back to the pleasures of the mind and begin our conversation.
As was said, we’ve heard, I think, from
our ministerial and politicians panel a moment ago,
lots of “this should happen, this should happen,
this is what we need.” And that’s exactly the
kind of political steer, political direction and urgency
which is needed, as we’ve been hearing
all week. It feels like it’s been the [unclear] of
AI to get things going. But clearly, saying that
things must happen is very different to making
them actually happen in practice, and that is
very much what we are about in this section of the program.
So let me begin with the question that
I think has, to some extent, precipitated this
frenzy of AI conversations this week, and ask you, Yoshua. Your International
AI Safety Report, it feels like some time ago
that that came out this year. I know, right?
And the scientific panel’s report both warned against advanced agents that could deceive
people... well, that happened... and act on their
own. Well, as we know, that happened this
summer. I know you’ve rushed out a thematic paper
from the scientific panel in time to guide the
conversations this week, which I urge everybody to
read if you haven’t already. But what can we
actually do about this if we want agents
to stop this deceitful behavior? What do we do?
All right, thanks for the question. So in this brief, you’ll see
we discuss three necessary conditions for the kind
of events we’ve seen during the summer.
And because they’re all necessary, society can play
on all of these factors to try to
prevent future things like this, and eventually loss of control. So first, the AIs
had a misaligned goal. They wanted to do something
that they shouldn’t be doing, and we can talk
about why and so on. But point is, it’s not
new. We’ve seen that in many other settings. AIs,
because of their training, have these kinds of bad goals sometimes.
Second, they need to have the capability, or
the intelligence, to actually achieve the goal,
given the possibility, given the tools, and given the third condition, which is
the environment in which the AI is running, like cybersecurity defenses, humans that are
checking what’s going on or not, are preventing
or not the carrying on of these plans, right?
So it’s important to see that you need
all three, and then you can think of, like,
what can we do about each of these things. And
a lot of people have been saying, oh, OpenAI
should have done, you know, better cybersecurity, should
not have removed the monitors. Sure, but
if capabilities continue and we don’t solve alignment,
it’s almost certain that there will be AI
smart enough to go through our defenses. In particular,
humans are always going to be a weak
link. And that’s true in cybersecurity in general, but
there were other events, for example, where the
AIs tried to convince someone from accepting,
you know, malicious code, for example. It was not
a cybersecurity obstacle. It was just a human, you
know, persuasion obstacle. So we should do these things,
but we have to deal with the other two.
So the capability factor is basically the reason why
a lot of people are asking for a pause,
or pacing. Make sure we don’t allow AIs
that are much more capable and, you know,
could do these bad things if we don’t solve
alignment. And then the other thing we could do,
of course, is solving alignment, which nobody knows how to do. But I think
it should be a priority, and that’s why I’ve been
working on this now for a couple of years, and
I created a nonprofit, LawZero, that has a
clear plan, actually, to solve this. But
in general, we need to think of these
three things and not just focus on one.
You think it is possible to solve alignment?
Yes. Excellent. Let’s all hold on to that.
But the companies are not even trying right now. Okay. Well,
if we have time, we’ll come back to incentives.
Sara, let me turn to you. The 20, actually
I think it’s now somewhere hovering close to 40,
country call that we heard earlier, that was convened by Finland and Norway.
One of the things that it suggests is
that states should explore a body that can verify,
and then convene for action when a set of agreed limits are crossed. Obviously,
the OECD has been one of the bodies that has
been tasked with implementing some of the AI principles
and agreements that do already exist. Do you think
that there are parts of this machinery that we
need that actually already exist, and which are
the things that we’re going to have to build?
Yeah, thank you for the question, and thanks for being
here, for being able to be here today. I
think we’ve already heard Ambassador, and also President Karis, mention earlier,
you know, we need a common vocabulary, at
least as a starting point. And again,
we work so closely with industry, policymakers and
researchers to reach consensus and a shared
understanding. So on agentic, we’ve already published a shared definition on this, and we’re
building on this already with a publication that
came out this week, just for UNGA, perfect timing,
already also documenting how organizations are actually deploying
agentic systems and what governance practices they’re putting
in place, and also to what extent,
you know, they’re needing new tools and so
on. And what we’re seeing in that paper
is that, to a large extent, existing governance tools are being adapted.
But, no surprises, sort of what the conversation is about here: the system for
verification and a shared understanding for risk management is what’s missing.
So I think, for that, of course, we
also have a number of other tools. The OECD
developed a framework for incident reporting that has already influenced standards bodies, you know,
working on standards. So those definitions, we also
see them kind of percolate through the system
and influencing broader frameworks, still voluntary. But again, the EU AI Act decided to
pick that up and implement it also in
its legal framework. So again, this requires that that’s
what states decide to do. So that’s one. And I
think on the side of risk management, you know,
we also work closely with companies on the HAIP, the Hiroshima Process Reporting Framework,
and by analyzing common trends in that kind
of reporting, hopefully governments will look to that
when they decide how to respond, so that, again,
we don’t come up with entirely new things that
aren’t interoperable with what’s already in place. So
I think that would be my hope.
Absolutely. I think interoperability is a word that
we come back to again and again in these
discussions. Jaan, I mean, Yoshua just raised the
issue of incentives, and, you know, companies
needing to want to create the kind of models which
solve alignment and so on. Or stop doing it. Or
stop doing it. Institutions and policy are one
way of creating incentives, positive or negative,
but clearly money and the bottom line is often the more persuasive incentive. What
kind of concrete incentives do you think could
make a frontier company accept outside limits,
before maybe we get to the point of law enforcing those limits?
Thank you. So unfortunately, I think that money doesn’t really motivate, at least directly,
these frontier companies anymore, because, like, $10 billion
is like small change for them now.
But of course, they do depend on revenue,
but now that the product is clearly demonstrated
that it’s very useful, it’s just very easy
to sell it unless there are some regulatory constraints.
So yes, I’m very happy with the Californian
efforts to actually put some kind of constraints
on the companies. But now, as demonstrated recently, there’s also a very different
motivator for these companies, which is that the employees are afraid now.
We just saw over 1,000 employees of the
frontier companies just said, like, please help us now.
So I think one thing that is not money, but
everybody can do, is think about, like, how can we
help them? Just let’s be empathetic. Like, they’re
afraid for their lives now. Their lives and ours.
Yes. Thank you. Okay, this has become quite dark , but rightly so.
Xiao Qian, China has its own AI safety governance
framework, we know, and has joined some of the
shared risk statements, and many of the individual
scientists, of course, share many of these same
concerns. Where do you sense that there is
strong consensus? We talked about shared scientific
consensus in the conversation earlier. Where do you
get a sense that there is a shared scientific
consensus between the scientific communities in China, in
Europe, in the US, and where do you
think there is a gap that some of the
communiqués that we have seen haven’t yet quite closed?
Well, this is really a good question, and thank
you very much for having me in this panel,
and I really believe it is important to have a Chinese perspective here.
According to this kind of common consensus, I
really believe we think that the international
cooperation on AI safety is really important, because
we know that all these kinds of AI risks
are not limited to only one country, and we should have cooperation here.
But the gap is that we don’t see
very efficient international cooperation on AI safety right now.
There are a lot of geopolitical tensions and misunderstandings. So we really hope
that there might be a kind of international platform, away from the political tension
and away from the politics, that people can
really work together on those important issues.
Yeah. Thank you. Thank you. And of course, we’re having this conversation
on the day that we’ve seen talks just
a few hundred miles down the road
in Washington on this very topic. Jaan, I
want to come back to you. You’ve funded AI
safety and independent evaluations, including groups like METR, for close to 20 years now.
That is pretty much the lifetime that most of us
have been talking about the AI industry at all.
To your knowledge, did any of that work
point to a mechanism that could have prevented this
summer’s incident? And if not, what do you think we should be doing differently?
So one thing is that I think it has been,
like, a kind of godsend for OpenAI to have
those incidents, because it’s just, like, almost in
one fell swoop, demonstrated three things that
have been super hard to tell the people, that
it’s coming. They just, like, didn’t believe it. Like,
one is that AI has volition. It will not follow
instructions; it will do its own thing. Second is
that the real dangers come from pre-deployment, not,
like, how do we diffuse AI and be
responsible, which is also important, but the real
serious risk will come before AI is deployed:
the lab leaks, so to speak. And the third one
is that the international borders will not save you,
will not protect you from the risks that
the labs are taking, as demonstrated with the
Australian hack. So yeah, it’s been really great. But to answer your question directly,
I really don’t... There’s one potential exception, which
is, in fact, one of the hosts
here, the Machine Intelligence Research Institute. They have been advocating that, look, this
idea of making AI as capable as possible
while using the fact that they are not capable
to control them, it’s just fundamentally flawed. It’s basic common sense.
So if we would have followed this common
sense, then yes, we would have prevented this incident.
Thank you. Xiao Qian, I want to come back to you on
a related point. The 2024 Beijing dialogue that
you took part in did draw a red line
that no AI system should improve itself without explicit human approval and assistance. Now,
we’ve been hearing many times this week that
self-improvement is on the horizon. Do you
think that that risk threshold still holds in
China, and do you think we can verify it?
Well, I, and also Professor Yoshua Bengio, was also at that meeting,
and I really believe that the Chinese AI
safety community has a very interactive dialogue
with the international community. And thank you, Professor
Bengio, you brought the people to China
and then had dialogues with Chinese scholars. So
I think, because now we are seeing more and
more incidents, and the urgency is much more than
in 2024... At that time, when you mentioned this
kind of existential risk and all these kinds of
red lines, I think that was quite new for
the Chinese scholars and Chinese scientists. But then,
with our understanding of AI risk getting
more and more, I mean, together with international
scientists, I think people got to know more about
this and are trying to work more together
with the international experts, like Yoshua Bengio.
So I really hope this kind of effort can continue,
and China is willing to be part of this effort.
I’m curious about how the AI community in
China has been discussing the events with OpenAI and
Hugging Face and the other related events. You
mean assessment? Is that part of the discussion?
I mean, we’re having those discussions here, but I wonder, is there something
happening in China in terms of discussing, you
know, the risks because of those incidents?
Yes, we do have a lot of internal
discussions on these risks, and shortly after this week,
we will go back and we will have, like,
safety people together to talk about this recent risk,
because a lot has happened right now. And
also, it is also a very interesting development:
there are more and more labs doing this kind
of evaluations and testing, or more labs on safety
things. So I think this kind of effort
is getting more and more momentum in China.
Yeah. I have one last question for you, Yoshua. You’re building Scientist AI at
LawZero, and you, correct me if I’m wrong,
are arguing that the real danger is autonomy
itself. And that’s something that I’ve heard again
and again this week. So, you know,
the plan that’s been suggested to slow the frontier, to pace agentic and self-improving
systems: are we just, and this is again
an analogy I’ve heard several times this week,
are we just slowing the walk towards the
cliff that we are all about to fall off?
And if not, what would the genuine limit
on autonomy that changes the conversation look like?
Okay. So what is really dangerous is uncontrolled
autonomy, when the AIs are autonomous and going
after goals that we didn’t choose, and often
actually go against our instructions, as we’ve
seen last summer. Unfortunately, there’s a lot of
commercial pressure and demand for AIs that
are autonomous, to do jobs that people do,
and, you know, it’s profitable. But there are things
you could do with systems that are completely
non-agentic. You can use them as a guardrail
against other agents. But you can also rethink how to
do agentic systems so that you don’t mix the
kind of honest understanding of how the world works, like science does, idealized science,
and choosing actions, which is what’s going on with reinforcement learning. So this is
one of the things we’re exploring at LawZero:
how having a completely non-agentic system that
doesn’t have an ego, it is not like us, you
know, doesn’t want anything, but is honest about its
beliefs based on the data, can be used to choose
actions which could be useful for society as well.
Thank you. We have two minutes left of this panel,
so I want to ask each of you just to give
me, like, two or three words on one thing that you
wish that policymakers thought about more when they’re making policy on
how to fix the problems with AI. What’s
one thing that frustrates you about the policy conversation
that you wish that we could bring up to the
fore? I’ll start with you, Sara, and work back.
I think in this moment, it would be,
again, to maintain a grounding in evidence,
and, I mean, I think the conversation about evaluation
and external verification needs to stay top of mind at this moment.
Thank you. Xiao Qian?
I would believe that the communication channel between
us and China on possible AI incidents
is really important now, and I hope we
could make some progress in this regard.
Yeah. So, like, I mean, up until recently, the
dismissal of loss of control was the big one,
but luckily now it seems to be melting. I think
the next challenge would be to explain to people
that this is not going to be constrained
to the digital realm. Like, AI would be like...
we’re going to share the environment with another species.
If you continue like that, we need to have
global discussions about loss of control risks, but also
the power that AI gives, and, connecting to the earlier panel,
how we can manage that power at the
same time as managing the risks globally.
Thank you. So I think with that, we
have a sense of the urgency of understanding the
risk and also of communicating about the risk, which I think brings us
perfectly to a conclusion of this panel. Thank
you all so much. That was absolutely fascinating.
